blocks.text: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in confused and drowsy two days after a gastrointestinal bleed. He has a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, and his plasma ammonia is raised. Ammonia is a potent neurotoxin; every day the liver converts a large nitrogen load from amino acid breakdown into harmless urea. This unit explains how it does so, and what happens when that machinery fails.

blocks.markdown: **The problem.** Breaking down amino acids releases nitrogen as ammonia (NH3/NH4+). Gut bacteria add more. Ammonia is highly toxic to the brain, so it is carried in the blood in non-toxic forms, mainly **glutamine** (from glutamine synthetase) and **alanine** (from muscle), to the liver, where it is converted to **urea**, which is soluble, non-toxic and excreted by the kidney. The liver is the only organ with a complete urea cycle.

blocks.title: Urea cycle (ornithine cycle)
blocks.text: The urea cycle is the liver pathway that converts two nitrogen atoms, one from free ammonia and one from aspartate, plus carbon from bicarbonate, into one molecule of urea. It is divided between the mitochondrial matrix and the cytosol, and ornithine is the carrier that is regenerated each turn.

rows: NH3 + HCO3- + 2 ATP to carbamoyl phosphate
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), activated by N-acetylglutamate
blocks.caption: Reactions of the urea cycle. Citrulline leaves the mitochondrion and ornithine returns through an ornithine transporter.

blocks.markdown: **Features to know.** CPS I (mitochondrial, uses ammonia) is the **rate-limiting, regulated** step and is allosterically activated by **N-acetylglutamate**, made from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase (stimulated by arginine); this couples urea synthesis to amino acid load. Do not confuse it with cytosolic CPS II, which makes carbamoyl phosphate for pyrimidine synthesis using glutamine. The second nitrogen enters as **aspartate** (step 3), and **fumarate** from step 4 links the cycle to the citric acid cycle. The cost is **4 high-energy phosphate bonds per urea**: 2 ATP in step 1 and 1 ATP converted to AMP plus pyrophosphate in step 3, which uses two bonds.

blocks.title: Where do the two nitrogens in urea come from?
blocks.prompt: Identify the source of each nitrogen atom and the carbon in one molecule of urea.

steps.text: Step 1 incorporates free ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate; this supplies the first nitrogen, and the carbon comes from bicarbonate.
Step 3 condenses citrulline with aspartate; this supplies the second nitrogen (aspartate's amino group).
Step 5 hydrolyses arginine to release urea with the carbon and both nitrogens, regenerating ornithine.

blocks.answer: One nitrogen from ammonia, one from aspartate, and the carbon from bicarbonate (CO2).

blocks.title: Nitrogen carried in urea
blocks.prompt: Urea is CO(NH2)2 with molar mass 60 g per mole and 28 g of nitrogen per mole. A patient excretes 24 g of urea in 24 hours. What mass of nitrogen is this?

steps.text: Each urea has two nitrogen atoms (2 x 14 = 28 g per mole).

blocks.answer: 11.2 g of nitrogen per day, which reflects the amount of amino acid nitrogen disposed of as urea.

blocks.markdown: **Urea cycle disorders.** An inherited defect in any enzyme (or in N-acetylglutamate synthase or the ornithine transporter) blocks ammonia detoxification and causes **hyperammonaemia**. The most common is **ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency**, which is **X-linked** (the others are autosomal recessive). In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria, spills into the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis, producing excess **orotic acid** in urine; plasma citrulline is low. In CPS I deficiency orotic acid is low. **Arginase deficiency** causes accumulation of arginine and progressive spastic paraparesis rather than neonatal collapse. Complete defects present in the first days of life after protein feeds begin: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, tachypnoea, seizures and coma, whereas partial defects present later during stress or high protein intake.

**Why ammonia damages the brain.** Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier. In astrocytes glutamine synthetase combines it with glutamate to make glutamine, which accumulates and draws in water, causing **astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema**. Ammonia also depletes glutamate (a neurotransmitter and the source of GABA) and alpha-ketoglutarate, which impairs the citric acid cycle and brain ATP supply. Early in hyperammonaemia the respiratory centre is stimulated, leading to **hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis**. Management (a pharmacology teaching summary): stop protein intake, give glucose to limit catabolism, use nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate), arginine where appropriate, and haemodialysis for severe cases.

rows: Neonatal collapse after feeds; high urinary orotic acid; low citrulline
Reduced hepatic mass and portosystemic shunting; ammonia from gut bypasses the liver
Confusion, flapping tremor; precipitated by GI bleed, infection, constipation or diuretics
Rapidly rising ammonia with coagulopathy and encephalopathy
blocks.caption: Causes of hyperammonaemia.

blocks.title: Interpreting a plasma ammonia result
blocks.text: Ammonia is unstable and is generated by red cells and plasma enzymes after sampling, so the sample must be taken without a prolonged tourniquet or fist clenching, put on ice and analysed promptly; delays give falsely high results. Reference intervals vary by laboratory and units (micromol per litre or microgram per decilitre). In cirrhosis, ammonia supports but does not diagnose hepatic encephalopathy and correlates imperfectly with its severity; a normal result makes encephalopathy from ammonia less likely, so look for other causes.

blocks.title: Converting an ammonia result between units
blocks.prompt: A laboratory reports plasma ammonia as 85 micrograms per decilitre. Convert it to micromol per litre (NH3 molar mass 17 g per mole).

steps.text: 85 micrograms per dL = 850 micrograms per litre.
Divide by molar mass: 850 / 17 = 50 micromol per litre.

points: The urea cycle converts ammonia and aspartate nitrogen into urea in liver mitochondria (CPS I, OTC) and cytosol (argininosuccinate synthetase, lyase, arginase), costing four high-energy phosphate bonds per urea.
CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate; OTC deficiency is X-linked, with raised urinary orotic acid and low citrulline.
Hyperammonaemia causes astrocyte swelling, depletion of glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate, and respiratory alkalosis; in cirrhosis it results from reduced hepatic function and shunting.
Ammonia samples must be handled carefully, and results interpreted with the clinical picture.

questions.stem: Which compound is the allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: N-acetylglutamate, made from acetyl-CoA and glutamate, activates CPS I.
distractorRationale.b: Citrulline is a cycle intermediate, not the activator.
distractorRationale.c: Fumarate is a product of argininosuccinate lyase and enters the citric acid cycle.
distractorRationale.d: Orotic acid is an intermediate of pyrimidine synthesis.

questions.explanation: CPS I is the regulated entry step of the cycle, activated by N-acetylglutamate. Its synthesis is stimulated by arginine and by high glutamate, linking urea production to the amino acid load.

questions.stem: Which of the following urea cycle enzymes is located in the mitochondrial matrix?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: OTC, like CPS I, is mitochondrial.

questions.explanation: The first two reactions (CPS I and OTC) occur in the mitochondrial matrix, and the final three reactions occur in the cytosol. Citrulline therefore has to be exported from mitochondria to continue the cycle.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old boy becomes lethargic, vomits and breathes rapidly after starting milk feeds. Plasma ammonia is greatly raised, plasma citrulline is low, and urine orotic acid is high. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: OTC deficiency leaves carbamoyl phosphate to spill into pyrimidine synthesis, raising orotic acid, while citrulline is low.
distractorRationale.b: CPS I deficiency also gives low citrulline, but orotic acid is low because carbamoyl phosphate is not made.
distractorRationale.c: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency gives raised argininosuccinate and citrulline, not low citrulline.
distractorRationale.d: Arginase deficiency raises arginine and usually presents with spasticity rather than neonatal collapse.

questions.explanation: High orotic acid with low citrulline and hyperammonaemia points to a block at OTC: carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and is diverted to orotic acid, and citrulline cannot be formed. In CPS I deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate itself is not made, so orotic acid is low.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains why hyperammonaemia causes cerebral oedema?

options.text: Astrocytes convert ammonia and glutamate to glutamine, which accumulates and draws in water
Ammonia is converted to urea inside neurons, raising osmolality
Ammonia blocks glutamine synthetase, so glutamate accumulates

questions.correctOptionText: Astrocytes convert ammonia and glutamate to glutamine, which accumulates and draws in water

distractorRationale.a: Correct: glutamine synthetase in astrocytes detoxifies ammonia but the osmotically active glutamine causes swelling.
distractorRationale.b: Ammonia does not dissolve membranes; its toxicity is metabolic and osmotic.
distractorRationale.c: Neurons and astrocytes have no urea cycle.
distractorRationale.d: Ammonia is a substrate of glutamine synthetase, not an inhibitor.

questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase in astrocytes removes ammonia by making glutamine, but the glutamine accumulates and is osmotically active, causing astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Ammonia also depletes glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate, impairing neurotransmission and brain energy metabolism.

questions.stem: In a patient with cirrhosis, which factor contributes most to a raised plasma ammonia?

options.text: Reduced functional hepatocyte mass and portosystemic shunting, so gut-derived ammonia bypasses urea synthesis

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced functional hepatocyte mass and portosystemic shunting, so gut-derived ammonia bypasses urea synthesis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the diseased liver converts less ammonia to urea, and shunting lets portal blood bypass it.
distractorRationale.b: Increased urea excretion would not raise ammonia.
distractorRationale.c: The urea cycle is impaired in liver failure, not overactive.
distractorRationale.d: Muscle uptake of ammonia would lower, not raise, blood levels.

questions.explanation: Cirrhosis reduces the number of working hepatocytes, and collateral vessels carry portal blood around the liver. Ammonia from gut bacteria and amino acid catabolism therefore reaches the systemic circulation and brain, precipitating hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: True or false: early hyperammonaemia typically causes hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis rather than metabolic acidosis.
questions.explanation: Ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre, so early hyperammonaemia produces tachypnoea and respiratory alkalosis. This helps distinguish urea cycle defects from organic acidaemias, which classically cause metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports a plasma ammonia of 170 micrograms per decilitre. Using a molar mass of 17 g per mole for NH3, convert the result to micromol per litre.
questions.explanation: 170 micrograms per decilitre is 1700 micrograms per litre. Dividing by 17 micrograms per micromole gives 100 micromol per litre, which would be well above most adult reference intervals (these vary between laboratories), so it must be interpreted in the clinical context.

questions.stem: A patient excretes 30 g of urea (molar mass 60 g per mole, two nitrogen atoms of 14 g per mole each) in 24 hours. What mass of nitrogen does this represent?
questions.explanation: Each mole of urea contains two nitrogen atoms, 28 g of nitrogen per 60 g of urea. Nitrogen = 30 x 28 / 60 = 14 g per day, which shows that urea is the main vehicle for disposing of amino acid nitrogen.

questions.stem: List the reactions of the urea cycle in order, naming each enzyme, and state in which cellular compartment each occurs.
markingGuide: CPS I: ammonia, bicarbonate and 2 ATP to carbamoyl phosphate, mitochondrial matrix, activated by N-acetylglutamate
OTC: carbamoyl phosphate plus ornithine to citrulline, mitochondrial matrix
Argininosuccinate synthetase: citrulline plus aspartate plus ATP to argininosuccinate, cytosol
Argininosuccinate lyase: argininosuccinate to arginine plus fumarate, cytosol
Arginase: arginine to urea plus ornithine, cytosol; ornithine returns to mitochondria
questions.explanation: The first two steps happen in the mitochondrion and the last three in the cytosol, which requires transport of citrulline out and ornithine back. Knowing the compartments is the key to understanding the enzyme-specific disorders.

questions.stem: Compare the causes of hyperammonaemia in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and in cirrhosis, explain why ammonia is neurotoxic, and describe two precautions needed when interpreting a plasma ammonia result.
markingGuide: OTC deficiency: X-linked enzymatic block; carbamoyl phosphate accumulates, causing orotic aciduria; neonatal collapse after protein feeds
Cirrhosis: loss of functional hepatocytes and portosystemic shunting allow gut-derived ammonia to bypass the liver
Ammonia crosses blood-brain barrier; astrocytes make glutamine, causing swelling and cerebral oedema
Depletion of glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate impairs neurotransmission and energy metabolism
Precaution: avoid tourniquet and fist clenching, put sample on ice and analyse quickly because in-vitro ammonia generation gives false highs
Precaution: interpret in clinical context since levels correlate imperfectly with encephalopathy severity and reference intervals and units vary
questions.explanation: Both conditions raise ammonia through failure of hepatic detoxification, but by different mechanisms: a single enzyme defect in OTC deficiency, and loss of function plus shunting in cirrhosis. Because ammonia is unstable, pre-analytical handling directly affects the result.
